Chapter 1: Project Overview & Academic Scope

1.1 Introduction

EventPulse (originally derived from the open-source Eventora-MERN repository by ShivaMani02) is a full-stack event discovery, reservation, and management platform engineered with the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React, Node.js).

In a typical commercial web development scenario, projects focus on visual flair, payment gateway webhooks, and third-party SaaS integrations. However, in an Advanced Databases (AD) collegiate evaluation, the primary objective is fundamentally different: demonstrating deep understanding of document-oriented data modelling, database-level concurrency control, query plan optimisation through indexing, multi-stage aggregation pipelines, and atomic updates.

The 30-Second Viva Introduction Script (Memorise this!):
"Good morning, Professor. EventPulse is an event discovery and reservation platform built on MongoDB and Express. While it provides a complete user experience for browsing events and reserving tickets, our primary academic contribution focuses on Advanced Database concepts: we engineered database-level atomic seat allocation using findOneAndUpdate with conditional predicates to prevent race conditions; we implemented three multi-stage aggregation pipelines for revenue and occupancy analytics; and we enforced data integrity using MongoDB partial unique indexes that block duplicate active bookings without preventing re-booking after cancellation."

1.3 Academic Boundaries and Intentional Choices

In accordance with collegiate academic standards, the project prioritises verifiability, code clarity, and explainability over black-box external services:

  • Self-Contained Database Seeding: Rather than relying on manual input, the database features an automated, idempotent seeding script (seed.js) that populates realistic synthetic events, users, and multi-status bookings.
  • Decoupled Payment Simulation: Rather than depending on an external sandbox (e.g., Stripe/Razorpay) that can fail due to expired webhooks or API limits during an oral examination, payments follow a deterministic state machine where confirmed bookings transition to paid status cleanly.
  • Database Integrity over Application-Memory Math: Many student projects calculate revenue by downloading thousands of records into an Express JavaScript array and looping over them. In EventPulse, 100% of revenue, occupancy, and status statistics are calculated inside MongoDB via aggregation pipelines.

Chapter 3: System Architecture & Request Flow

3.1 End-to-End MERN Tier Interaction

EventPulse implements a decoupled 3-tier web architecture. The presentation layer (Vite + React) communicates exclusively with the application layer (Express.js on Node.js) over stateless HTTP/2 REST endpoints formatted in JSON. The backend communicates with the persistence layer (MongoDB) over binary TCP wire protocol using Mongoose ODM.

Figure 3.1: EventPulse 3-Tier Layered Architecture Diagram with Inter-Layer Communication Protocols.

3.2 Step-by-Step Request Lifecycle Example: Reserving a Seat

To understand how data flows through the application, consider what happens when a student clicks the "Book Ticket" button on an event:

  1. User Action: The user clicks "Book Ticket" in EventDetail.jsx.
  2. Client Interceptor: The custom Axios client in client/src/utils/axios.js intercepts the outgoing request, inspects localStorage.getItem('token'), and attaches Authorization: Bearer <token> to the HTTP header.
  3. Network Transmission: The browser issues a POST /api/bookings request with payload { eventId: "6ad138..." }.
  4. Route Matching: Express router in server/routes/bookings.js matches the path and executes the middleware chain.
  5. Authentication Guard: verifyToken middleware in server/middleware/auth.js extracts the Bearer header, validates the cryptographic signature using jwt.verify(token, JWT_SECRET), and sets req.user = decodedToken.
  6. Controller Execution: createBooking in server/controllers/bookingController.js executes.
  7. Atomic Database Update: The controller executes: 
    const event = await Event.findOneAndUpdate(
  { _id: eventId, availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } },
  { $inc: { availableSeats: -1 } },
  { new: true }
);
  8. Database Execution: MongoDB locates the event document via index scan, verifies that availableSeats > 0, decrements the seat counter atomically, and releases the document-level write lock.
  9. Booking Record Creation: The controller creates and saves a new Booking document with userId = req.user.id, status = 'confirmed', and amount = event.ticketPrice.
  10. Response Dispatch: Express serializes the newly created booking to JSON and responds with HTTP status 201 Created.
  11. UI Update: React receives the response, updates local state, displays a success notification, and decrements the visible seats badge.

Chapter 5: Frontend Architecture (React, SPA, Tailwind)

5.1 React Single Page Application (SPA) Design

The frontend is structured around React 18 and Vite. Rather than performing full-page browser reloads for every action, React Router dynamically mounts components into the root DOM node based on client-side URL changes.

5.2 Global Authentication State via React Context

Authentication state is managed centrally in client/src/context/AuthContext.jsx using the React Context API. This prevents "prop drilling" and makes user data accessible everywhere: 

// client/src/context/AuthContext.jsx (Excerpt)
export const AuthProvider = ({ children }) => {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(() => {
    const savedUser = localStorage.getItem('user');
    return savedUser ? JSON.parse(savedUser) : null;
  });

  const login = async (email, password) => {
    const res = await api.post('/auth/login', { email, password });
    localStorage.setItem('token', res.data.token);
    localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify(res.data));
    setUser(res.data);
    return res.data;
  };

  const logout = () => {
    localStorage.removeItem('token');
    localStorage.removeItem('user');
    setUser(null);
  };

  return (
    <AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, login, logout }}>
      {children}
    </AuthContext.Provider>
  );
};

5.3 Automatic Bearer Token Authorization via Axios Interceptor

To prevent writing repetitive authorization headers in every single API call, client/src/utils/axios.js configures a single Axios client: 

// client/src/utils/axios.js
import axios from 'axios';

const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL || 'http://localhost:5000/api',
});

api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('token');
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

export default api;

Chapter 7: Database Design — Mongoose Schemas & Relationships

7.1 Document-Oriented Data Modelling Rationale

In a traditional Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) like MySQL or PostgreSQL, strict schema tables and third-normal-form (3NF) normalization require foreign key tables and heavy multi-table SQL joins.

In MongoDB, data is stored as flexible, self-describing BSON (Binary JSON) documents. For EventPulse, a hybrid referenced model was selected:

  • Independent Collections: users, events, and bookings are stored in separate collections because events and users have independent lifecycles.
  • Foreign Reference Keys: The bookings collection acts as a joining document containing userId (referencing users._id) and eventId (referencing events._id).
  • Fast Reads with Targeted Lookups: When a user browses events, MongoDB queries only the events collection directly from B-tree index caches without joining any user records. When analytical reports are requested, MongoDB executes server-side $lookup joins.
Figure 7.1: MongoDB Entity-Relationship Architecture with Mongoose Schemas, Foreign References & Indexes.

Chapter 8: Database Operations & Worked CRUD Tracing

8.1 Code Walkthrough: Safe Seat Reservation

The following annotated snippet from server/controllers/bookingController.js illustrates how EventPulse implements concurrency-safe updates: 

// server/controllers/bookingController.js (createBooking)
exports.createBooking = async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { eventId } = req.body;
        const userId = req.user.id; // Extracted securely from verified JWT

        // 1. ATOMIC CONDITIONAL UPDATE:
        // MongoDB matches document ONLY if availableSeats > 0,
        // and decrements availableSeats by 1 in a single atomic write.
        const event = await Event.findOneAndUpdate(
            { _id: eventId, availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } },
            { $inc: { availableSeats: -1 } },
            { new: true }
        );

        if (!event) {
            return res.status(400).json({ 
                message: 'Event is fully booked or no longer available' 
            });
        }

        // 2. CREATE BOOKING DOCUMENT:
        const booking = new Booking({
            userId,
            eventId,
            amount: event.ticketPrice,
            status: 'confirmed',
            paymentStatus: event.ticketPrice === 0 ? 'paid' : 'not_paid'
        });

        await booking.save();
        res.status(201).json(booking);
    } catch (error) {
        // Handle MongoDB E11000 duplicate key error (Partial Unique Index)
        if (error.code === 11000) {
            return res.status(400).json({ 
                message: 'You already have an active booking for this event.' 
            });
        }
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Server error processing booking' });
    }
};

8.2 Code Walkthrough: Guarded Cancellation

When a user cancels a booking, seats must only be restored if the booking was genuinely confirmed. If the booking was pending or already cancelled, incrementing seats would create "ghost capacity": 

// server/controllers/bookingController.js (cancelBooking)
exports.cancelBooking = async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const booking = await Booking.findById(req.params.id);
        if (!booking) return res.status(404).json({ message: 'Booking not found' });

        // Ensure user owns booking or is admin
        if (booking.userId.toString() !== req.user.id && req.user.role !== 'admin') {
            return res.status(403).json({ message: 'Unauthorized' });
        }

        if (booking.status === 'cancelled') {
            return res.status(400).json({ message: 'Booking is already cancelled' });
        }

        const wasConfirmed = booking.status === 'confirmed';
        booking.status = 'cancelled';
        await booking.save();

        // ONLY RESTORE SEAT IF PREVIOUS STATUS WAS CONFIRMED
        if (wasConfirmed) {
            await Event.findByIdAndUpdate(booking.eventId, { 
                $inc: { availableSeats: 1 } 
            });
        }

        res.json({ message: 'Booking cancelled successfully', booking });
    } catch (error) {
        res.status(500).json({ message: 'Error cancelling booking' });
    }
};

Chapter 9: Booking Lifecycle, Concurrency & Seat Consistency

9.1 The Concurrency Race Condition Problem

In many college web projects, seat reservation is implemented using a naive two-step read-then-write approach: 

// NAIVE ANTI-PATTERN (PRONE TO RACE CONDITIONS):
const event = await Event.findById(eventId);
if (event.availableSeats > 0) {
    event.availableSeats = event.availableSeats - 1; // RACE CONDITION WINDOW!
    await event.save();
}

Why this fails: If EventPulse has 1 remaining seat, and User Alice and User Bob submit booking requests at the exact same millisecond:

  1. Alice's thread reads event.availableSeats = 1.
  2. Bob's thread reads event.availableSeats = 1 before Alice's write completes.
  3. Alice executes save() and sets availableSeats to 0.
  4. Bob executes save() and also sets availableSeats to 0.
  5. Result: 2 confirmed tickets were sold for 1 physical seat, causing an overbooking disaster.

9.2 The EventPulse Atomic Solution

EventPulse eliminates this race condition by delegating the predicate check and arithmetic operation directly to the MongoDB WiredTiger storage engine: 

Event.findOneAndUpdate(
  { _id: eventId, availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } },
  { $inc: { availableSeats: -1 } }
)

Under WiredTiger's document-level concurrency lock, MongoDB checks availableSeats > 0 and executes $inc: -1 in an indivisible atomic step. The second concurrent request fails the { availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } } filter and receives null, cleanly blocking the overbooking.

Figure 9.1: Concurrency Control and Booking Lifecycle State Machine.

Chapter 10: Authentication, Authorisation & Security Flow

10.1 Salted Password Hashing via Bcrypt

Passwords are never stored in plaintext. In server/controllers/authController.js, passwords pass through bcrypt with a work factor of 10: 

const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(10);
const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash(password, salt);

10.2 JSON Web Token (JWT) Stateless Authorization

Upon valid credential verification, the server signs a cryptographic JWT payload: 

const token = jwt.sign(
  { id: user._id, role: user.role },
  process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'fallback_secret',
  { expiresIn: '30d' }
);

10.3 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Guard Middleware

Endpoints are guarded by combining verifyToken and checkRole: 

// server/middleware/auth.js
const verifyToken = (req, res, next) => {
  const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1];
  if (!token) return res.status(401).json({ message: 'Access Denied: No token' });

  try {
    const verified = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
    req.user = verified;
    next();
  } catch (err) {
    res.status(400).json({ message: 'Invalid or expired token' });
  }
};

const checkRole = (role) => (req, res, next) => {
  if (req.user.role !== role) {
    return res.status(403).json({ message: 'Forbidden: Insufficient privileges' });
  }
  next();
};

Chapter 11: Advanced Database Concepts Demonstrated

11.1 Summary of Core AD Concepts

Advanced Database Concept Implementation in EventPulse Examiner Viva Question it Answers
Atomic Updates Event.findOneAndUpdate({ availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } }, { $inc: { availableSeats: -1 } }) "How do you prevent race conditions and overbooking when multiple users click book simultaneously?"
Partial Unique Indexes BookingSchema.index({ userId: 1, eventId: 1 }, { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { status: 'confirmed' } }) "How do you prevent duplicate active bookings without preventing the user from re-booking after cancellation?"
Multi-Stage Aggregations Pipelines using $match, $group, $lookup, $reduce, $project, and $sort. "Why is calculating revenue in MongoDB aggregation superior to calculating it in Node.js array loops?"
Multi-Faceted Queries Booking.aggregate([{ $facet: { ... } }]) computing 7 KPIs in a single query pass. "How do you avoid multiple round-trip network calls when rendering a dashboard with multiple metrics?"
Query Execution Plans Demonstrated via .explain('executionStats') proving IXSCAN index usage. "How do you prove to me that your MongoDB queries are actually using your indexes?"

Chapter 12: Aggregation Pipelines & Index Query Plans

Figure 12.1: Flow Architecture of the Three Aggregation Pipelines Implemented in EventPulse.

12.1 Pipeline 1: Booking Status Summary (/api/analytics/booking-status)

Business Goal: Provide the operations team with a breakdown of bookings by status (confirmed, pending, cancelled) alongside total financial value requested and paid/unpaid counts. 

// server/controllers/analyticsController.js
const summary = await Booking.aggregate([
    {
        $group: {
            _id: '$status',
            count: { $sum: 1 },
            paidCount: {
                $sum: { $cond: [{ $eq: ['$paymentStatus', 'paid'] }, 1, 0] }
            },
            unpaidCount: {
                $sum: { $cond: [{ $eq: ['$paymentStatus', 'not_paid'] }, 1, 0] }
            },
            totalAmountRequested: { $sum: '$amount' }
        }
    },
    {
        $project: {
            _id: 0,
            status: '$_id',
            count: 1,
            paidCount: 1,
            unpaidCount: 1,
            totalAmountRequested: 1
        }
    },
    { $sort: { count: -1 } }
]);

12.2 Pipeline 2: Event Revenue & Occupancy Summary (/api/analytics/event-summary)

Business Goal: Cross-reference events with booking records via a server-side $lookup join to calculate confirmed paid revenue and occupancy percentage without counting pending or unpaid requests. 

// server/controllers/analyticsController.js (Excerpt)
const eventSummaries = await Event.aggregate([
    {
        $lookup: {
            from: 'bookings',
            localField: '_id',
            foreignField: 'eventId',
            as: 'bookings'
        }
    },
    {
        $project: {
            title: 1,
            category: 1,
            totalSeats: 1,
            availableSeats: 1,
            ticketPrice: 1,
            totalBookings: { $size: '$bookings' },
            confirmedBookings: {
                $size: {
                    $filter: {
                        input: '$bookings',
                        as: 'b',
                        cond: { $eq: ['$$b.status', 'confirmed'] }
                    }
                }
            },
            // STRICT VERIFIED REVENUE CALCULATION:
            // Only bookings with status == 'confirmed' AND paymentStatus == 'paid'
            verifiedRevenue: {
                $reduce: {
                    input: '$bookings',
                    initialValue: 0,
                    in: {
                        $add: [
                            '$$value',
                            {
                                $cond: [
                                    {
                                        $and: [
                                            { $eq: ['$$this.status', 'confirmed'] },
                                            { $eq: ['$$this.paymentStatus', 'paid'] }
                                        ]
                                    },
                                    '$$this.amount',
                                    0
                                ]
                            }
                        ]
                    }
                }
            },
            occupancyRate: {
                $round: [
                    {
                        $multiply: [
                            { $divide: [{ $subtract: ['$totalSeats', '$availableSeats'] }, '$totalSeats'] },
                            100
                        ]
                    },
                    1
                ]
            }
        }
    },
    { $sort: { verifiedRevenue: -1 } }
]);

12.3 MongoDB Indexing Architecture & Query Plans

EventPulse defines targeted B-tree indexes to optimize filtering and enforce business constraints:

Collection Index Key Pattern Type Query Plan Justification
events { category: 1, date: 1 } Compound B-Tree Optimizes GET /api/events?category=Technology. Replaces full collection scan (COLLSCAN) with index range scan (IXSCAN).
bookings { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 } Compound B-Tree Accelerates user booking history queries in reverse chronological order.
bookings { eventId: 1, status: 1 } Compound B-Tree Accelerates event-level booking lookups and status filtering.
bookings { userId: 1, eventId: 1 } (confirmed) Partial Unique Enforces uniqueness ONLY where status == 'confirmed'. Prevents duplicate tickets while allowing re-booking if cancelled.
Verification via explain('executionStats'): Running node server/scripts/verify-indexes-and-queries.js outputs execution statistics showing totalDocsExamined: 0 and stage: "IXSCAN", proving that queries read directly from index memory rather than scanning documents.

14.2 Known Technical Boundaries & Honest Viva Disclosures

  • Multi-Document ACID Transactions: MongoDB multi-document transactions require a MongoDB Replica Set. Because basic collegiate local development typically runs a standalone mongod instance, EventPulse utilizes atomic single-document operations (findOneAndUpdate) rather than multi-document transaction sessions.
  • Payment Gateway Simulation: To guarantee that a student can complete a live presentation without internet or payment gateway sandbox failures, payments are simulated as internal deterministic state transitions.

Chapter 16: Comprehensive Viva Preparation (35 Q&As)

Topic 1: MongoDB & Database Architecture

Q1: Why did you choose MongoDB over a relational database like MySQL for this project?
Answer: MongoDB stores data as flexible, self-describing BSON documents. For an event booking platform with variable event categories, embedded metadata, and rapid read requirements, MongoDB's document model allows events to be retrieved in a single read without multi-table joins. Furthermore, MongoDB's aggregation framework allows complex analytical metrics to be calculated directly in the storage engine.

Q2: What is Mongoose and what is its role?
Answer: Mongoose is an Object Data Modelling (ODM) library for MongoDB and Node.js. It provides schema validation, type casting, middleware hooks, index synchronization, and model abstraction over raw MongoDB collections (defined in server/models/).

Q3: How do you handle relationships in MongoDB?
Answer: EventPulse uses a hybrid referencing approach. In Booking.js, we store userId and eventId as mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId with ref declarations. For analytics, we join collections using the $lookup aggregation stage.

Topic 2: Concurrency & Data Integrity

Q4: How do you prevent overbooking when two users book the last seat simultaneously?
Answer: In bookingController.js, we execute Event.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: eventId, availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } }, { $inc: { availableSeats: -1 } }). Because MongoDB executes document updates atomically under the WiredTiger storage engine, the predicate check and seat decrement occur indivisibly, preventing race conditions.

Q5: What is a Partial Unique Index and why did you use it?
Answer: A standard unique index on (userId, eventId) would permanently prevent a user from booking an event ever again even if they cancelled their previous ticket. A Partial Unique Index adds a partialFilterExpression: { status: 'confirmed' }, meaning uniqueness is only enforced while the ticket is active.

Q6: How is seat restoration handled upon cancellation?
Answer: In cancelBooking, the server checks if the previous status was 'confirmed' before executing $inc: { availableSeats: 1 }. If the booking was already pending or cancelled, seats are not restored, preventing seat inflation.

Topic 3: Aggregation Pipelines

Q7: What aggregation stages did you use in Pipeline 1?
Answer: In /api/analytics/booking-status, we used $group to bucket documents by status, $cond inside $sum to calculate paid vs unpaid counts, $project to reshape fields, and $sort to order by count descending.

Q8: How does Pipeline 2 calculate verified revenue?
Answer: In /api/analytics/event-summary, we join bookings via $lookup, and use $reduce with a conditional $and check ensuring that only bookings where status == 'confirmed' AND paymentStatus == 'paid' contribute to the revenue sum. Pending or unpaid bookings are excluded.

Q9: What is the $facet stage used for in your overview endpoint?
Answer: $facet allows multi-faceted aggregation, processing multiple pipeline branches within a single stage over the same incoming documents. This allows EventPulse to compute total revenue, confirmed bookings, and pending counts in a single network round-trip.

Topic 4: Indexing & Query Optimization

Q10: What indexes did you create and how do they help?
Answer: We created compound index { category: 1, date: 1 } on events to speed up filtering by category and date; compound index { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 } on bookings for fast user history lookups; and partial unique index { userId: 1, eventId: 1 } for concurrency safety.

Q11: How do you prove that an index is working?
Answer: We append .explain('executionStats') to the Mongoose query. In the returned query execution plan, stage: "IXSCAN" confirms an index scan was used instead of a COLLSCAN (collection scan).

Topic 5: Questions the Examiner May Ask About Implementation Quirks

Q12: Why didn't you use multi-document ACID transactions with session.startTransaction()?
Answer: MongoDB multi-document transactions require a multi-node Replica Set. In local collegiate setups and standalone Docker deployments, replica sets are often not configured. We achieved concurrency safety without replica set overhead by using atomic single-document updates with conditional predicates.

Q13: Why did you rebrand from Eventora to EventPulse?
Answer: To clearly delineate our enhanced, database-focused academic contribution from the upstream repository, while ensuring complete isolation from unrelated personal or production databases.

Q14: Where does the JWT token live in the client?
Answer: In localStorage. It is extracted by an Axios request interceptor and injected into the Authorization: Bearer header for every authenticated request.

Q15: What happens if MongoDB goes down while the server is running?
Answer: Mongoose's connection buffer holds requests temporarily while attempting to reconnect. If reconnection fails within the timeout window, Mongoose throws a MongooseServerSelectionError, which our Express route error handlers catch to return HTTP 500 responses.

Chapter 17: Glossary, Quick Reference & Summary Sheets

17.1 Important Technical Terms

  • BSON: Binary JSON. The binary-encoded serialization format used by MongoDB to store documents and perform remote procedure calls.
  • IXSCAN: Index Scan. An execution plan state proving that MongoDB retrieved records using an in-memory B-tree index rather than scanning every document on disk.
  • COLLSCAN: Collection Scan. An inefficient execution plan state where MongoDB scans every document in a collection because no suitable index was found.
  • Partial Unique Index: An index that only enforces uniqueness on documents that satisfy a specified filter expression (e.g. status: 'confirmed').
  • Atomic Operation: An operation that completes entirely or not at all, with no possibility of another concurrent process seeing an intermediate state.
  • $lookup: A MongoDB aggregation stage performing an equality left outer join between two collections in the same database.

17.2 One-Page Quick Revision Sheet

Topic Key Fact to State in Viva Code Reference
Seat Allocation Atomic findOneAndUpdate with { availableSeats: { $gt: 0 } } and { $inc: { availableSeats: -1 } } server/controllers/bookingController.js
Active Duplicate Guard MongoDB Partial Unique Index on (userId, eventId) with filter status: 'confirmed' server/models/Booking.js
Seat Restoration Guard Restores seat on cancellation ONLY if previous status was confirmed. cancelBooking in bookingController.js
Pipeline 1 (Status) $group by status, conditional $cond paid/unpaid accumulation, $sort /api/analytics/booking-status
Pipeline 2 (Revenue) $lookup join, strict $reduce verified revenue (paid + confirmed only), occupancy rate /api/analytics/event-summary
Pipeline 3 (Popularity) $match: { status: 'confirmed' }, $group by eventId, $lookup title/price, $sort /api/analytics/event-popularity
Overview KPIs Single-pass $facet aggregation computing 7 KPIs in one network trip. /api/analytics/overview
